reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: Stabilization with Portland Cement
sections.summary: Portland cement can modify (improve quality) or stabilize (transform into a cemented mass) a soil; the amount of cement depends on which objective governs. Types, water, gradation, and content-determination procedures follow in the child sections.
sections.body: Portland cement can be used either to modify and improve the quality of the soil or to transform the soil into a cemented mass with increased strength and durability. The amount of cement used will depend upon whether the soil is to be modified or stabilized.
key_points: Cement can either modify (improve quality) or stabilize (cement into a mass) a soil
Required cement content differs depending on which objective governs
Full design procedure covers cement type, water, gradation, modification content, and stabilization content
sections.applicability: Governing section for all portland-cement stabilization/modification design in this UFC.

sections.title: Types of Portland Cement
sections.summary: Type I/IA cement was traditionally used; Type II offers greater sulfate resistance at similar cost; Type III (high early strength, finer particles) cures faster and can give higher strength in certain soils. Specifications: ASTM C150.
sections.body: Several different types of cement have been successfully used for stabilizing soils. Type I normal portland cement and Type IA air-entraining cements were used extensively in the past with similar results. At the present time, Type II cement has greater sulfate resistance obtained while the cost is often the same. High early strength cement (Type III) has been found to give higher strength in certain soils and cures much faster than Type I or Type II. Type III cement has a finer particle size than the other cement types. Chemical and physical property specifications for portland cement can be found in ASTM C150, Standard Specification for Portland Cement.
key_points: Type I / Type IA: traditional normal / air-entraining cement
Type II: greater sulfate resistance, often similar cost to Type I
Type III: high early strength, finer particle size, faster cure, higher strength in some soils
Specification reference: ASTM C150
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the specific portland cement type for a stabilization project, e.g. sulfate-resistant or fast-curing needs.

sections.title: Water for Hydration
sections.summary: Potable water is normally used for cement stabilization, although seawater has been found satisfactory.
sections.body: Potable water is normally used for cement stabilization, although seawater has been found to be satisfactory.
key_points: Potable water is the standard mixing water
Seawater has been found to be a satisfactory alternative
sections.applicability: Applies to sourcing hydration water for cement-stabilized soil mixing, including remote or coastal sites.

sections.title: Gradation Requirements (Cement)
sections.summary: Gradation requirements for cement-stabilized base and subbase courses are given in Table 3-1, with separate envelopes for base (1.5in through No.200) and subbase (1.5in through No.200, no 0.75in check).
sections.body: Gradation requirements for cement-stabilized base and subbase courses are in Table 3-1.
key_points: Base course gradation envelope: 1.5in=100%, 0.75in=70-100%, No.4=45-70%, No.40=10-40%, No.200=0-20%
Subbase course gradation envelope: 1.5in=100%, No.4=45-100%, No.40=10-50%, No.200=0-20%
tables: Table 3-1: Gradation Requirements for Cement-Stabilized Base and Subbase Courses
sections.applicability: Applies to material selection/testing for cement-stabilized base or subbase courses before mix design begins.

sections.title: Cement Content for Modifying Soils
sections.summary: Cement content for soil MODIFICATION (as opposed to full stabilization) is determined for one of three objectives: improved plasticity, improved gradation, or reduced swell potential; frost-area considerations apply an additional check.
sections.body: The amount of cement required to improve the quality of a soil through modification depends on the objective: reducing plasticity index (PI), improving gradation of a granular soil, or reducing swell potential of expansive soils. Each objective has its own trial-and-error test procedure, detailed in the child sections. Regardless of objective, check the cement content found for modification against the strength criteria for stabilization (Sec 3-1.5, Table 2-1) to determine whether it happens to also qualify for reduced-thickness design.
key_points: Three modification objectives: improved plasticity (Sec 3-1.4.1), improved gradation (Sec 3-1.4.2), reduced swell potential (Sec 3-1.4.3)
Frost-area soils require an additional freeze-thaw check (Sec 3-1.4.4)
A modification-level cement content should still be checked against Table 2-1 strength criteria in case it also qualifies as stabilization
sections.applicability: Container section; see 3-1.4.1 through 3-1.4.4 for each cement-modification objective's test procedure.

sections.title: Improved Plasticity
sections.summary: Lime is generally preferred to reduce PI; if unavailable, cement can be used. Prepare soil-cement samples at various treatment levels, test PI on the minus-No.40 fraction, then adjust to total-sample-weight design cement content via A=100BC.
sections.body: In a majority of cases, lime is preferred over soil cement to reduce the PI or control expansive behavior. If lime is not locally or economically available for a project, it is possible to use cement to reduce the plasticity. Do not design, specify, or install soil cement to reduce the PI of a soil without prior authorization by the Pavements DWG. The amount of cement required to improve the quality of the soil through modification is determined by the trial-and-error approach: prepare successive samples of soil-cement mixtures at different treatment levels and determine the PI of each mixture (ASTM D4318). The minimum cement content that yields the desired PI is selected, but since it was determined based on the minus No. 40 (0.425 mm) sieve material, this value is adjusted to find the design cement content based on total sample weight, expressed as A = 100BC, where A = design cement content (percent total weight of soil), B = percent passing No. 40 sieve (decimal), and C = percent cement required to obtain the desired PI of minus No. 40 material (decimal).
key_points: Lime is generally preferred for PI reduction; cement is a fallback when lime is unavailable
Requires prior Pavements DWG authorization to use cement for PI reduction
Trial-and-error: test PI (ASTM D4318) on soil-cement mixtures at various treatment levels, on the minus-No.40 fraction
Adjust the minus-No.40 result to total-sample design cement content via A = 100BC (equation_cement_content_modifying_soils)

equations.description: Design cement content adjusted from the minus-No.40-sieve trial result to a percentage of total soil sample weight: A = 100*B*C

sections.applicability: Applies when the design objective is reducing PI (e.g. of an expansive or high-plasticity soil) via cement, not full stabilization.

sections.title: Improved Gradation
sections.summary: If the modification objective is improving a granular soil's gradation by adding fines, conduct particle-size analysis (ASTM D7928) on samples at various treatment levels to find the minimum acceptable cement content.
sections.body: If the objective of modification is to improve the gradation of a granular soil through the addition of fines then conduct a particle size analysis (ASTM D7928, Standard Test Method for Particle-Size Distribution (Gradation) of Fine-Grained Soils Using the Sedimentation (Hydrometer) Analysis) on samples at various treatment levels to determine the minimum acceptable cement content.
key_points: Applies when the objective is gradation improvement (adding fines to a granular soil), not PI reduction
Test method: ASTM D7928 particle-size distribution (sedimentation/hydrometer) at various cement treatment levels
Select the minimum cement content that achieves the target gradation
sections.applicability: Applies when the design objective is improving a granular soil's gradation via cement addition.

sections.title: Reduced Swell Potential
sections.summary: Cement can reduce swell in expansive soils (less effectively/more expensively than lime). Mold samples at various cement contents, soak 4 days (ASTM D4546), and select the lowest content that eliminates/minimizes swell; then check UCS for stabilization criteria.
sections.body: Portland cement may reduce swell potential of certain expansive soils. However, portland cement is not as effective as lime in reducing swell potential and may be considered too expensive for this application. Determining cement content to reduce the swell potential of fine-grained plastic soils can be accomplished by molding several samples at various cement contents and soaking the specimens along with untreated specimens for four days. The lowest cement content that eliminates the swell potential or reduces the swell characteristics to the minimum is the design cement content. Procedures for measuring swell characteristics of soils are found in ASTM D4546-14e1, Standard Test Methods for One-Dimensional Swell or Collapse of Soils. Check the cement content found to accomplish soil modification to determine whether it provides an unconfined compressive strength great enough to qualify for a reduced thickness design in accordance with criteria established for soil stabilization.
key_points: Cement is less effective than lime for swell reduction and may be more expensive
Test procedure: mold samples at various cement contents, soak 4 days alongside untreated specimens (ASTM D4546-14e1)
Design cement content = lowest content that eliminates or minimizes swell
Cross-check the resulting cement content's UCS against Table 2-1 stabilization strength criteria for possible thickness-reduction credit
sections.applicability: Applies when the design objective is controlling swell/shrink of an expansive fine-grained plastic soil via cement (secondary to lime).

sections.title: Frost Areas (Cement Modification)
sections.summary: Cement-modified soil in frost areas requires additional 12-cycle freeze-thaw testing (ASTM D560, omitting wire-brushing) beyond the standard modification procedure, to determine frost susceptibility for subgrade design.
sections.body: Cement-modified soil may also be used in frost areas but, in addition to the procedures for mixture design described in paragraphs 3-1.5.1 through 3-1.5.5, cured specimens are subjected to the 12 freeze-thaw cycles prescribed by ASTM D560, Standard Test Methods for Freezing and Thawing Compacted Soil-Cement Mixtures (but omitting wire-brushing). Follow the determination of frost design soil classification by means of standard laboratory freezing tests. If cement-modified soil is used as subgrade, its frost susceptibility, determined after freeze-thaw cycling, is used as the basis of the pavement thickness design if the reduced subgrade design method is applied.
key_points: Additional requirement in frost areas: 12 freeze-thaw cycles per ASTM D560, omitting wire-brushing
Frost susceptibility classification determined via standard laboratory freezing tests
If cement-modified soil is used as subgrade, its post-cycling frost susceptibility governs a reduced-subgrade thickness design
sections.applicability: Applies to cement-modified soil intended for use in a seasonal-frost region, on top of the standard modification procedure.

sections.title: Cement Content for Stabilized Soil
sections.summary: Five-step design procedure for cement-stabilized soil: (1) classify soil, (2) select estimated cement content from Table 3-2, (3) moisture-density tests at that content +/-2%, (4) UCS and durability tests (triplicate, 7-day cure), (5) select the lowest content meeting both criteria.
sections.body: Determine the design cement content for cement-stabilized soils using the following five-step procedure. Step 1: determine gradation, Atterberg limits, and classification of the untreated soil (ASTM D7928, D4318, D2487). Step 2: using the soil classification, select an estimated cement content for moisture-density tests from Table 3-2. Step 3: conduct moisture-density tests at the estimated cement content and at contents 2 percent above and below it (ASTM D558 to prepare, ASTM D1557 modified-effort compaction) to determine maximum dry density and optimum water content at each content; this sets the allowable field density range (cement-treated density is often higher than untreated due to cement's high specific gravity). Step 4: prepare triplicate samples at the Step-2 content and at +/-2 percent for unconfined compression and durability tests, compacted at the design field density/moisture (e.g. 97+/-2% of max density at 9+/-2% moisture); prepare per ASTM D1632 (4-in x 8-in mold if >35% retained on No. 4), cure 7 days in a humid room, then test 3 specimens for UCS (ASTM D1633) and 3 for durability (wet-dry ASTM D559 or freeze-thaw ASTM D560, as appropriate) and determine frost susceptibility per UFC 3-260-02. Step 5: compare the average UCS and durability results with Tables 2-1 and 2-2; the lowest cement content meeting BOTH the strength and durability requirement is the design cement content. If durability is met but not strength, the mixture is a 'modified' soil, not 'stabilized'. If neither is met, select a higher cement content and repeat Steps 3-4.
key_points: Step 1: classify soil (gradation ASTM D7928, Atterberg ASTM D4318, USCS ASTM D2487)
Step 2: select estimated cement content from Table 3-2 (table_3_2_cement_content_by_soil) by USCS class
Step 3: moisture-density tests (ASTM D558/D1557) at estimated content +/-2%
Step 4: triplicate UCS (ASTM D1633, 7-day cure) and durability (ASTM D559/D560) tests at estimated content +/-2%
Step 5: design cement content = lowest content meeting BOTH Table 2-1 strength AND Table 2-2 durability; meeting only durability = 'modified' not 'stabilized'
tables: Table 3-2: Cement Requirements for Various Soils
Table 2-1: Minimum Unconfined Compressive Strength for Cement-, Lime-, Lime-Cement, and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash-Stabilized Soils
sections.applicability: The primary cement-stabilization (as opposed to modification) mix-design procedure; used whenever full strength/durability stabilization credit is sought.

sections.title: Stabilization with Lime
sections.summary: Lime-treated fine-grained soils typically show decreased plasticity, improved workability, and reduced volume change, though not all soils show improved strength. Reactivity depends on soil type, lime type/percentage, and curing conditions; always test.
sections.body: Generally, lime-treated, fine-grained soils exhibit decreased plasticity, improved workability, and reduced volume change characteristics. However, not all soils exhibit improved strength characteristics. Note that the properties of soil-lime mixtures are dependent on many variables: soil type, lime type, lime percentage, and curing conditions (time, temperature, moisture) are the most important. Perform preliminary lime reactivity testing on each soil type intended for use on a project, as not all soil-lime combinations are reactive. Prior to designing a stabilization program to treat a shrink/swell soil, thoroughly examine the geological/geotechnical conditions with respect to groundwater and runoff water; eliminate or mitigate the water source that causes expansive soil to swell rather than over-treating the soil, requiring the initial design study to be robust with specific attention to water conditions above and below the surface. Designing lime treatment based on potential vertical rise (PVR) can overestimate actual vertical rise and over-prescribe lime treatment depth/quantity once the water source is mitigated; conversely, if the water source is not mitigated, the stabilization treatment may not handle a surge of water flow into the expansive zone.
key_points: Lime-treated fine-grained soils: decreased plasticity, improved workability, reduced volume change (strength improvement not guaranteed)
Reactivity depends on soil type, lime type, lime percentage, and curing conditions -- always test reactivity first
Mitigating the groundwater/runoff source of swell is preferred over over-prescribing lime treatment
PVR-based lime treatment design can overestimate required lime once the water source is mitigated
sections.applicability: Governing section for all lime stabilization/modification design in this UFC.

sections.title: Types of Lime
sections.summary: Common lime products: hydrated high-calcium lime, monohydrated dolomitic lime, calcitic quicklime, dolomitic quicklime. Hydrated lime is most common (less caustic). Quicklime dosage may be reduced only at Pavements DWG direction. Spec: ASTM C977.
sections.body: Various forms of lime have been successfully used as soil-stabilizing agents for many years. However, the most commonly used products are hydrated high-calcium lime, monohydrated dolomitic lime, calcitic quicklime, and dolomitic quicklime. Hydrated lime is used most often because it is much less caustic than quicklime. Under certain circumstances, the quantity of lime may be reduced if quicklime is used in lieu of hydrated lime; however, only reduce the amount of lime prescribed by the mix design at the direction of the Pavements DWG. Specifications for quicklime and hydrated lime may be found in ASTM C977, Standard Specification for Quicklime and Hydrated Lime for Soil Stabilization.
key_points: Common products: hydrated high-calcium lime, monohydrated dolomitic lime, calcitic quicklime, dolomitic quicklime
Hydrated lime is most common (less caustic than quicklime)
Reducing prescribed lime quantity when substituting quicklime requires Pavements DWG direction
Specification reference: ASTM C977
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the specific lime product form for a stabilization project.

sections.title: Gradation Requirements (Lime)
sections.summary: Consider lime stabilization only for soils containing a minimum of 25 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve.
sections.body: Consider lime stabilization of soils containing a minimum of 25 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve.
key_points: Minimum gradation threshold for lime candidacy: >= 25% passing the No. 200 sieve
sections.applicability: Screening criterion applied before proceeding with lime content design (Sec 3-2.3).

sections.title: Lime Content for Lime-Modified Soils
sections.summary: Five-step lime-content procedure: (1) pH test (ASTM D6276) to find initial design lime content (lowest content giving pH>=12.4), (2) moisture-density tests, (3) triplicate UCS/durability samples cured 28 days at 73F (or accelerated 120F/48hr with 73F check), (4) UCS (ASTM D2166) plus freeze-thaw if frost applies, (5) select lowest content meeting strength+durability.
sections.body: The amount of lime required to improve the quality of a soil is determined through the same trial-and-error process used for cement-modified soils. Highly weathered soils may require higher lime content than usually specified by previous guideline documents. Step 1: the preferred method for determining initial design lime content is the pH test (ASTM D6276, Standard Test Method for Using pH to Estimate the Soil-Lime Proportion Requirement for Soil Stabilization). Several lime-soil slurries are prepared at different lime treatment levels (e.g. 2, 4, 6, 8 percent lime) and the pH of each is measured; the lowest lime content at which a pH of at least 12.4 (the pH of free lime) is obtained is the initial design lime content -- the minimum required for pozzolanic reactions to occur. Step 2: using the initial design lime content, conduct moisture-density tests (ASTM D3551 to prepare, ASTM D1557 to test) to determine maximum dry density and optimum water content. Step 3: prepare triplicate UCS and durability samples at the initial design content and at 2 and 4 percent above it (preferred method) or 2 percent above/below (alternate method), per ASTM D3551, molded to expected field density/moisture; cure in a sealed container (73 degF / 23 degC for 28 days preferred; accelerated 120 degF / 49 degC for 48 hours also acceptable but requires an additional 73 degF/28-day check, since overly-high accelerated temperatures can form pozzolanic compounds unlike those developed in the field). Step 4: test 3 specimens for UCS (ASTM D2166/D2166M); if frost design applies, subject 3 additional specimens to 12 freeze-thaw cycles (ASTM D560, omitting wire brushing) and determine frost susceptibility per UFC 3-260-02. Step 5: compare results with Tables 2-1 and 2-2; the lowest lime content meeting BOTH the UCS and durability requirement (and frost susceptibility, if applicable) is the design lime content. If durability is met but not strength, the mixture is a 'modified' soil. If neither is met, select a higher lime content and repeat Steps 1-5.
key_points: Step 1: pH test (ASTM D6276) at trial lime contents (e.g. 2/4/6/8%); initial design content = lowest reaching pH >= 12.4
Step 2: moisture-density tests (ASTM D3551/D1557) at the initial design content
Step 3: triplicate UCS/durability samples cured 28 days at 73F (or accelerated 120F/48hr, with a 73F/28-day check)
Step 4: UCS per ASTM D2166; freeze-thaw (ASTM D560, 12 cycles, no wire brushing) if frost design applies
Step 5: design lime content = lowest content meeting BOTH Table 2-1 strength AND Table 2-2 durability requirements
Highly weathered soils may need higher lime content than typical guideline values
tables: Table 2-1: Minimum Unconfined Compressive Strength for Cement-, Lime-, Lime-Cement, and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash-Stabilized Soils
sections.applicability: The primary lime-stabilization mix-design procedure; used whenever full strength/durability stabilization credit is sought via lime.

sections.title: Stabilization with Lime-Fly Ash (LF) and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash (LCF)
sections.summary: LF/LCF stabilizes coarse-grained soils with little/no fines by supplying an agent (fly ash) that lime can react with, forming a hardened cementitious matrix; commonly used for base/subbase materials.
sections.body: Stabilization of coarse-grained soils having little or no fines can often be accomplished by the use of LF or LCF combinations. Fly ash, also termed coal ash, is a mineral residual from the combustion of pulverized coal. It contains silicon and aluminum compounds that, when mixed with lime and water, form a hardened cementitious mass capable of obtaining high compressive strengths. Lime and fly ash in combination can often be successfully used to stabilize granular materials since the fly ash provides an agent with which the lime can react; thus, LF or LCF stabilization is often appropriate for base and subbase course materials.
key_points: Fly ash (coal combustion residual) supplies silicon/aluminum compounds that react with lime and water to form a hardened cementitious mass
LF/LCF is especially suited to coarse-grained soils with little or no fines, which lime alone cannot stabilize
Common application: base and subbase course materials
sections.applicability: Governing section for LF and LCF stabilization design; applies to granular materials otherwise unreactive with lime alone.

sections.title: Types of Fly Ash
sections.summary: Class C fly ash ('high lime,' from lignite/subbituminous coal) is self-cementitious but sensitive; Class F ('low lime,' from anthracite/bituminous coal) requires added lime. Volcanic ash, rice hull ash, and GGBFS slag are also used where available.
sections.body: Fly ash is classified according to the type of coal from which the ash was derived. Class C fly ash is derived from the burning of lignite or subbituminous coal and is often referred to as 'high lime' ash because it contains a high percentage of lime; it is self-reactive or cementitious in the presence of water in addition to being pozzolanic, but has proven sensitive and difficult at times. Class F fly ash is derived from the burning of anthracite or bituminous coal and is sometimes referred to as 'low lime' ash; it requires the addition of lime to form a pozzolanic reaction. Volcanic ash, rice hull ash (Type N natural pozzolans), and slag (ground-granulated blast-furnace slag, GGBFS) may be used as stabilizers where available, and have been used successfully in certain geographic locations for many years.
key_points: Class C ('high lime', lignite/subbituminous coal): self-cementitious AND pozzolanic, but sensitive/difficult in practice
Class F ('low lime', anthracite/bituminous coal): requires added lime for a pozzolanic reaction
Alternative pozzolans: volcanic ash, rice hull ash (Type N), ground-granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBFS)
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a fly ash source/class for LF or LCF stabilization design.

sections.title: Evaluation of Fly Ash
sections.summary: Fly ash used for stabilization is acceptable when it meets ASTM C593 (Standard Specification for Fly Ash and Other Pozzolans for Use with Lime for Soil Stabilization).
sections.body: Fly ash used for stabilization is acceptable quality when it meets the requirements indicated in ASTM C593, Standard Specification for Fly Ash and Other Pozzolans for Use with Lime for Soil Stabilization.
key_points: Acceptance specification: ASTM C593
sections.applicability: Quality-acceptance gate for any fly ash source proposed for LF/LCF stabilization.

sections.title: Gradation Requirements (LF/LCF)
sections.summary: LF and LCF stabilization are useful only in soils with PI < 25 and less than 50 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve.
sections.body: LF and LCF stabilization are useful only in soils with a PI less than 25 and less than 50 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve.
key_points: Applicability threshold: PI < 25 and < 50% passing the No. 200 sieve
sections.applicability: Screening criterion applied before proceeding with LF/LCF content design (Sec 3-3.4/3-3.5).

sections.title: Selection of Lime-Fly Ash Content for LF and LCF Mixtures
sections.summary: Unlike lime/cement, LF design varies lime-fly-ash percentage, moisture, and lime:fly-ash ratio; the matrix (fly ash+lime+minus-No.4 fines) must 'float' the coarse aggregate. Step 1 finds optimum fines content (+2%); Step 2 finds the best lime:fly-ash ratio (1:3, 1:4, 1:5).
sections.body: Design with LF is different from stabilization with lime or cement. For a given combination of materials (aggregate, fly ash, and lime), factors such as percentage of lime-fly ash, moisture content, and the lime-to-fly-ash ratio can be varied. Engineering characteristics such as strength and durability are directly related to the quality of the matrix material (fly ash, lime, and minus-No.4 aggregate fines): the matrix must 'float' the coarse aggregate particles by overfilling the void spaces between them; the quantity of matrix required for maximum dry density of the total mixture is the optimum fines content. Step 1: determine the optimum fines content that gives maximum density -- run moisture-density tests (ASTM D1557) at increasing fly ash content (starting ~10 percent, in ~2 percent increments up to ~20 percent, on the minus-0.75in fraction), then select the design fly ash content 2 percent above the density-maximizing value (an alternate single-point-compaction method is also given). A subsequent moisture-density test at the design fly ash content sets the optimum water content and maximum dry density for the LF-stabilized soil. Step 2: determine the lime-to-fly-ash ratio giving the highest strength/durability -- prepare triplicate specimens at the design fly ash content and optimum water content, at LF ratios of 1:3, 1:4, and 1:5 (about 1 percent portland cement may optionally be added). Step 3: test UCS (ASTM D2166/D2166M) on 3 specimens; if frost design applies, subject 3 more to 12 freeze-thaw cycles (ASTM D560, no wire brushing) and determine frost susceptibility per UFC 3-260-02. Step 4: compare results with Tables 2-1 and 2-2; the design LF content is the lowest-lime-content ratio meeting both strength and durability (and frost, if applicable). If neither requirement is met, select a different LF content or add cement and repeat Steps 2-4.
key_points: LF design varies three things at once: lime-fly-ash percentage, moisture content, and the lime:fly-ash ratio
Matrix material (fly ash + lime + minus-No.4 fines) must 'float' the coarse aggregate; target = optimum fines content + 2%
Step 1: moisture-density tests at increasing fly ash content (~10-20%, on minus-0.75in fraction) to find optimum fines content
Step 2: triplicate specimens at lime:fly-ash ratios 1:3, 1:4, 1:5 (optionally + ~1% cement)
Steps 3-4: UCS (ASTM D2166) and freeze-thaw (ASTM D560) testing; design LF content = lowest-lime ratio meeting Tables 2-1/2-2
tables: Table 2-1: Minimum Unconfined Compressive Strength for Cement-, Lime-, Lime-Cement, and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash-Stabilized Soils
sections.applicability: The primary LF (lime-fly ash) content mix-design procedure for coarse-grained soils with little or no fines.

sections.title: Selection of Cement Content for LCF Mixtures
sections.summary: Portland cement can be added to LF for improved strength/durability, generally 1-2%, following the same procedure as LF design starting at Step 2; cement may replace or supplement lime but total fines content must be maintained.
sections.body: Portland cement may also be used in combination with LF for improved strength and durability. If it is desired to incorporate cement into the mixture, follow the same procedures indicated for LF design but include cement beginning at step 2. Generally, about 1 to 2 percent cement is used. Cement may be used in place of or in addition to lime; however, maintain the total fines content. Conduct strength and durability tests on samples at various LCF ratios to determine the combination that gives best results.
key_points: Cement addition follows the LF design procedure starting at Step 2 (the lime:fly-ash ratio step)
Typical cement addition: 1-2%
Cement can replace or supplement lime, but total fines content must be maintained
Design LCF ratio is selected from strength/durability testing across various LCF combinations
sections.applicability: Applies when adding cement to an LF mixture (i.e. designing LCF rather than plain LF) for improved strength/durability.

sections.title: Stabilization with Bitumen and Polymer Emulsion
sections.summary: Bitumen/polymer stabilization is fundamentally a waterproofing mechanism (film coating) plus, in cohesionless materials, adhesion/cementing between grains. Design is based on stability and gradation (bitumen) or UCS alone (polymer); freeze-thaw/wet-dry durability tests don't apply.
sections.body: Stabilizing soils and aggregates with asphalt and polymer emulsion differs greatly from stabilizing soils with cement and lime. The basic mechanism involved in stabilizing fine-grained soils is a waterproofing phenomenon: soil particles or agglomerates are coated with an asphalt or polymer film that prevents or slows water penetration, which typically results in a decrease in soil strength if untreated. Asphalt/polymer stabilization can also improve durability by resisting water-driven volume changes. In non-cohesive materials (sands, gravel, crushed gravel, crushed stone), two mechanisms are active: waterproofing (membrane preventing water penetration) and adhesion (the binder cements soil particles together, increasing cohesion and shear strength). Criteria for bitumen-stabilized soils are based almost entirely on stability and soil gradation requirements; for polymer emulsions, criteria are based solely on unconfined compressive strength. Freeze-thaw and wet-dry durability tests are not applicable for asphalt- or polymer-stabilized mixtures.
key_points: Primary mechanism: waterproofing (film coating prevents water penetration and associated strength loss)
Secondary mechanism in cohesionless materials: adhesion (binder cements particles together, increasing shear strength)
Bituminous design criteria: stability and gradation; polymer design criteria: unconfined compressive strength only
Freeze-thaw and wet-dry durability tests do NOT apply to asphalt- or polymer-stabilized mixtures
sections.applicability: Governing section for bituminous and polymer emulsion stabilization design; covers sand-bitumen, gravel-bitumen, and bitumen-lime material types.

sections.title: Types of Bituminous-Stabilized Soils and Bitumen
sections.summary: Three bituminous-stabilized soil types: sand bitumen, gravel/crushed-aggregate bitumen, and bitumen-lime (for high-PI material, PI>10). Bitumen type (asphalt cement, cutback, or emulsion) depends on soil, location, construction method, and weather; emulsions are generally preferred for safety/environmental reasons.
sections.body: Sand bitumen is a mixture of sand and bitumen in which sand particles are cemented together for increased stability. Gravel or crushed aggregate bitumen is a mixture of bitumen and well-graded gravel/crushed aggregate providing, after compaction, a stable waterproof base/subbase-quality mass. Bitumen lime is a mixture of soil, lime, and bitumen exhibiting characteristics of the above types; lime is used with material having a high PI (above 10). Bituminous stabilization is generally accomplished using asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, or asphalt emulsions, with the type chosen based on soil type, location, construction method, and weather. The most viscous liquid asphalt that can be readily mixed is generally most satisfactory; central-plant high-quality mixes use viscosity-grade asphalt cements, while in-place mixing typically uses liquid asphalts (cutbacks/emulsions). Emulsions are preferred over cutbacks for safety, reduced energy consumption, and environmental regulations. Typical bitumen grades by aggregate gradation: open-graded aggregate uses RC-250/RC-800/MC-3000 or MS-2/CMS-2 emulsions; well-graded aggregate with little/no minus-No.200 material uses RC/MC-250/800, SC-250/800, or MS-2/CMS-2/SS-1/CSS-1 emulsions; aggregate with considerable fines uses MC-250/800, SC-250/800, or SS-1/SS-01h/CSS-1/CSS-1h emulsions. The simplest bituminous stabilization is surface-applying liquid asphalt to an unbound aggregate road, using SC-70/SC-250/MC-70/MC-250 or slow-setting emulsions.
key_points: Sand bitumen: sand cemented together by bitumen for increased stability
Gravel/crushed aggregate bitumen: well-graded aggregate + bitumen -> stable waterproof base/subbase mass
Bitumen lime: soil + lime + bitumen; lime used for high-PI material (PI > 10)
Bitumen forms: asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, asphalt emulsion -- emulsions generally preferred (safety, energy, environmental)
Bitumen grade selection depends on aggregate gradation (open-graded vs. well-graded vs. fines-rich) per the source's grade tables
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing the bituminous-stabilized soil type and specific bitumen grade for a given aggregate gradation and construction method.

sections.title: Soil Gradation (Bituminous)
sections.summary: Recommended soil gradations for bituminous stabilization are given in Table 3-3 (subgrade materials) and Table 3-4 (base/subbase materials, four bands by nominal maximum aggregate size).
sections.body: The recommended soil gradations for subgrade materials and base or subbase course materials are shown in Tables 3-3 and 3-4, respectively.
key_points: Table 3-3: gradation envelope for bituminous-stabilized subgrade materials (3in through No.200)
Table 3-4: gradation envelopes for bituminous-stabilized base/subbase materials, four bands by nominal max aggregate size (1.5in, 1in, 0.75in, 0.5in)
tables: Table 3-3: Recommended Gradations for Bituminous-Stabilized Subgrade Materials
Table 3-4: Recommended Gradations for Bituminous-Stabilized Base and Subbase Materials
sections.applicability: Applies to material selection/testing for bituminous-stabilized subgrade, base, or subbase courses before mix design.

sections.title: Mix Design (Bituminous)
sections.summary: Design of bituminous-stabilized base/subbase is per UFC 3-250-01. For subgrade stabilization, a preliminary cutback-asphalt content can be estimated from the aggregate's fractional retention on the No.50/100/200 sieves and percent solvent, then finalized via Marshall Stability testing (min. 500 lb for subgrades).
sections.body: Guidance for the design of bituminous-stabilized base and subbase courses is in UFC 3-250-01. For subgrade stabilization, the following equation may be used for estimating the preliminary quantity of cutback asphalt to be selected: p = [0.02(a) + 0.07(b) + 0.15(c) + 0.20(d)] / (100-S) * 100, where p = percent cutback asphalt by weight of dry aggregate; a, b, c, d = percent of mineral aggregate in successively finer sieve bands (retained on No.50; passing No.50/retained No.100; passing No.100/retained No.200; passing No.200); S = percent solvent. The preliminary quantity of emulsified asphalt for subgrade stabilization can be determined from Table 3-5. Select the final design content of cutback or emulsified asphalt based on Marshall Stability Test results (ASTM D6927); minimum recommended Marshall Stability for subgrades is 500 lb (227 kg). If a soil does not show increased stability with reasonable bituminous additions, modify the soil gradation or use another bituminous material type. Poorly graded materials may be improved by adding suitable fines containing considerable minus-No.200 material. The amount of bitumen required increases with increasing percentage of finer sizes.
key_points: Base/subbase mix design: per UFC 3-250-01 (not detailed in this UFC)
Subgrade preliminary cutback content: p = [0.02a+0.07b+0.15c+0.20d]/(100-S)*100 (equation_cutback_asphalt_content_estimate)
Subgrade preliminary emulsified-asphalt content: Table 3-5 (table_3_5_emulsified_asphalt_requirements), by percent passing No.200 and No.10 sieves
Final design content selected from Marshall Stability Test (ASTM D6927); minimum 500 lb (227 kg) for subgrades
Increasing fines content generally increases the required bitumen dosage

equations.description: Preliminary cutback-asphalt content for subgrade stabilization: p = [0.02(a)+0.07(b)+0.15(c)+0.20(d)]/(100-S)*100

sections.applicability: The primary bituminous-content mix-design procedure, particularly for subgrade stabilization where a closed-form preliminary estimate is offered.

sections.title: Polymer Emulsion
sections.summary: Follow manufacturer dosage guidance as a starting point, then a trial-and-error procedure similar to cement/lime (moisture-density -> triplicate UCS at initial content +/-1% -> select lowest content averaging >400 psi). Cement can be added, typically starting at 1%.
sections.body: Due to the wide variety of polymer emulsion properties, it is best to follow the manufacturer's recommendations for starting dosage amounts. The recommended polymer-content procedure is similar to cement/lime stabilization: Step 1, determine gradation/Atterberg limits/classification (ASTM D6913/D6913M, D4318, D2487); Step 2, select an initial polymer content per manufacturer recommendation for moisture-density tests (ASTM D1557); Step 3, using the initial content, determine the water added from the emulsion (by percent solids) and conduct moisture-density tests (ASTM D558 to prepare, ASTM D1557 to test) to find MDD/OMC; Step 4, prepare triplicate UCS samples at the initial content and +/-1 percent, molded per ASTM D1632 at design field density/moisture, cured 7 days at 77 degF (25 degC) in 50 percent humidity, tested per ASTM D1633; Step 5, ensure the average of 3 tests exceeds 400 psi (2.76 MPa) -- the lowest polymer content meeting this is the design polymer content; if not met, adjust content and repeat Steps 1-4. Portland cement may be added in combination with polymer emulsion (same procedure, beginning with a manufacturer-suggested polymer content); if combined, the initial trial cement is 1 percent and must not exceed the design polymer emulsion content. The polymer provides strength, flexibility, and water resistance while cement provides strength and helps the emulsion cure by reacting with the emulsion water.
key_points: Start with manufacturer-recommended dosage; procedure otherwise mirrors cement/lime trial-and-error design
Moisture-density tests (ASTM D558/D1557) at the initial trial content, accounting for water contributed by the emulsion itself
Triplicate UCS samples (ASTM D1632/D1633) at initial content +/-1%, cured 7 days at 77F/50% humidity
Design polymer content = lowest content with average UCS > 400 psi (2.76 MPa)
Cement can be added (typically starting at 1%, not exceeding the design polymer content) for additional strength and cure assistance
sections.applicability: The primary polymer-emulsion (and optional polymer+cement) content mix-design procedure.

sections.title: Stabilization with Lime-Cement and Lime-Bitumen
sections.summary: Combination stabilizers let one additive compensate for the other's limitations, e.g. lime makes plastic clay friable so cement or asphalt can then be mixed in properly; more costly than single stabilizers but sometimes economical where aggregate is scarce.
sections.body: The advantage in using combination stabilizers is that one of the stabilizers in the combination compensates for the lack of effectiveness of the other in treating a particular aspect or characteristic of a given soil. For instance, in clay areas devoid of base material, lime has been used jointly with other stabilizers, notably portland cement or asphalt, to provide acceptable base courses: since portland cement or asphalt cannot be successfully mixed with plastic clays, lime is incorporated into the soil to make it friable, permitting the cement or asphalt to be adequately mixed. While this practice may be more costly than conventional single-stabilizer methods, it may still be economical where base aggregate costs are high. Two combination stabilizers are considered: lime-cement and lime-asphalt.
key_points: Combination stabilizers let one additive compensate for the other's limitations on a given soil
Common case: lime first makes a plastic clay friable, enabling proper mixing of cement or asphalt afterward
More costly than single-stabilizer methods but can be economical where base aggregate is expensive/scarce
Two combinations covered: lime-cement (Sec 3-5.1) and lime-asphalt (Sec 3-5.2)
sections.applicability: Applies to clay-rich sites devoid of quality base aggregate, where neither cement/asphalt nor lime alone is practical.

sections.title: Lime-Cement
sections.summary: Lime is added first (alone or as an initial additive) primarily to improve workability by reducing plasticity to acceptable levels; design lime content is the minimum achieving that. Design cement content follows the standard cement-stabilized-soil procedure (Sec 3-1).
sections.body: Lime can be used as an initial additive with portland cement or alone as the primary stabilizer. The main purpose of lime is to improve workability characteristics, mainly by reducing the plasticity of the soil. The design approach is to add enough lime to improve workability and reduce the PI to acceptable levels. The design lime content is the minimum that achieves desired results. The design cement content is arrived at following procedures for cement-stabilized soils in paragraph 3-1.
key_points: Lime's role: improve workability by reducing PI to an acceptable level (not the primary strength-provider)
Design lime content = the minimum amount achieving adequate workability/PI
Design cement content follows the standard Sec 3-1 cement-stabilized-soil procedure
sections.applicability: Applies to plastic clay soils where lime pretreatment is needed before cement can be effectively mixed in.

sections.title: Lime-Asphalt
sections.summary: Lime (about 1-2%) is used as an initial additive with asphalt as the primary stabilizer, mainly to improve workability and act as an anti-stripping agent (neutralizing acidic chemicals interfering with asphalt bonding). Follow standard bituminous procedures (Sec 3-4) for the asphalt content.
sections.body: Lime can be used as an initial additive with asphalt as the primary stabilizer. The main purpose of lime is to improve workability characteristics and act as an anti-stripping agent. In the latter capacity, the lime acts to neutralize acidic chemicals in the soil or aggregate that tend to interfere with bonding of the asphalt. Generally, about 1 to 2 percent lime is all that is needed for this objective. When asphalt is the primary stabilizer, follow the procedures for asphalt-stabilized materials in paragraph 3-4.
key_points: Lime's role: improve workability and act as an anti-stripping agent (neutralizes acids interfering with asphalt bonding)
Typical lime dosage for this purpose: 1-2%
Asphalt content design follows the standard Sec 3-4 bituminous-stabilization procedure
sections.applicability: Applies to soils/aggregates prone to asphalt stripping, where a small lime addition improves asphalt bonding.

sections.title: Lime Treatment of Expansive Soils
sections.summary: Expansive soils (swell > 3%) can be treated with lime; swell potential correlates with plasticity (Table 3-6). Design lime content is the minimum reducing swell to < 1%, per ASTM D4546 swell testing; typical maximum treatment depth is 2-3 ft without soil removal.
sections.body: Expansive soils as defined for pavement purposes are those that exhibit swell in excess of 3 percent. Expansion is characterized by heaving of a pavement or road when water is imbibed in the clay minerals. The plasticity characteristics of a soil are often a good indicator of the swell potential, as indicated in Table 3-6. If it has been determined that a soil has potential for excessive swell, lime treatment may be appropriate. Lime will reduce swell in an expansive soil to a greater or lesser degree, depending on the activity of the clay minerals present. The amount of lime to be added is the minimum amount that will reduce swell to acceptable limits, less than 1 percent swell, using the swell-test procedure of ASTM D4546-14e1. The maximum depth that lime can be incorporated is typically limited by construction equipment; however, 2 to 3 ft (0.6-0.9 m) generally is the maximum depth that can be treated directly without removal of the soil. Once the design lime content has been determined, perform testing to verify the intended lime stabilization will also prevent soil expansion, since the lime content necessary to reduce PI is not always suitable to control shrink/swell.
key_points: Expansive soil definition (for pavement purposes): swell in excess of 3%
Table 3-6 (table_3_6_swell_potential) correlates LL/PI with swell potential (Low/Marginal/High)
Design lime content = minimum amount reducing swell to < 1% (ASTM D4546-14e1 swell test)
Typical maximum treatable depth without soil removal: 2-3 ft (0.6-0.9 m)
The PI-reduction lime content and the swell-control lime content are NOT always the same -- verify swell control separately
sections.applicability: Applies specifically to expansive (high-swell) soils, as a design objective distinct from ordinary strength/durability stabilization.

sections.title: Stabilization with Fibers
sections.summary: Fiber stabilization is an emerging field; polypropylene fibers are most common. Follow manufacturer dosage guidance; fibers add toughness/ductility rather than stiffness and are best combined with an adhesive (cement, bitumen, or polymer). Starting dosage ~0.1%, max ~0.8%.
sections.body: Fiber stabilization in soils is an emerging field. Polypropylene fibers are the most common for soil applications. It is best to follow manufacturer's recommendations for starting dosage amounts for the classification and gradation of the soil. Fibers are very efficient at adding toughness to the soil; they usually do not add stiffness but improve ductility. Fibers may be used alone but are recommended to be used with an adhesive (cement, bitumen, or polymer); fibers blended with cement reduce shrinkage cracking. Criteria on the amount of fibers to use are not available at this time, but general guidelines apply; refer to UFC 3-220-08FA, Engineering Use of Geotextiles, for additional guidance. Monofilament and tape fibers are more efficient for rapid stabilization; fibrillated fibers require extensive mixing (multiple passes) to effectively defibrillate. Without adhesives, fibers rely exclusively on mechanical interlock, friction, and fiber entanglement with soil particles for anchorage; a high-surface-area fiber (tape) may be more efficient in fine-grained clay than in coarse-grained gravel, where fewer soil grains contact the fiber. Fiber amounts vary with length, denier, and morphology; typical fiber lengths range 0.5-3 in (13-76 mm). Longer fibers are recommended if no adhesives are used but generally hamper construction (more difficult to mix, considerable 'balling'). Shorter fibers (<1 in / 25 mm) are recommended when using adhesives, since the adhesive helps create a composite fiber network. A recommended fiber starting dosage is 0.1 percent, with a maximum of 0.8 percent; increased fiber amounts may reduce soil stiffness and become difficult to mix.
key_points: Polypropylene fibers are most common; follow manufacturer starting-dosage guidance
Fibers add toughness/ductility, not stiffness; best combined with an adhesive (cement, bitumen, or polymer)
Monofilament/tape fibers stabilize faster than fibrillated fibers (which need extensive mixing to 'open')
Typical fiber length range: 0.5-3 in (13-76 mm); shorter (<1in) preferred with adhesives, longer preferred without
Recommended dosage: 0.1% starting, 0.8% maximum -- higher amounts reduce stiffness and mixing workability
Reference for geosynthetic fiber guidance: UFC 3-220-08FA
sections.applicability: Applies whenever fiber reinforcement (alone or combined with another additive) is the chosen stabilization approach.
